ch45.anchor: the British legation secretary Ernest Satow
ch45.note: Ernest Satow (1843–1929), the young British interpreter and diplomat whose fluent Japanese and Satsuma-Chōshū sympathies made him an influential figure in the last Tokugawa years; he served under Minister Sir Harry Parkes. His memoir, quoted here, is A Diplomat in Japan (1921); Shiba cites it from the Japanese translation. Satow’s eyewitness detail — the Fushimi fire seen from Osaka — is genuine, and corroborates the scale of the blaze.

The decisive battle of 1600, in which Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Eastern army crushed the coalition (the “Western army”) loyal to the Toyotomi, opening the way to the Tokugawa shogunate. Shiba’s point is the parallel: at Sekigahara, as at Toba-Fushimi, the numerically stronger side lost for want of will, only a few units fighting in earnest. The comparison frames Toba-Fushimi as the mirror-image undoing of what Sekigahara had built.

In the sixth month of 1867 the Shinsengumi, until then hired swords in Aizu’s pay, were formally taken into direct shogunal service, its officers granted the standing of hatamoto (see the note on hatamoto at chapter 2). This is why Nagakura, a deserter from Matsumae by birth, could now lord it over the recruited “infantry” as their social superior. The “Ōgobangumi” (Great Guard) was one of the shogunate’s standing hatamoto guard corps.

Matsudaira Masatada (1844–1868 in office as commander; d. 1897), daimyo of Ottō and nominal commander-in-chief of the shogunal field army at Toba-Fushimi. “Buzen-no-kami” is a court title, not a personal name. His repeated orders to fall back, relayed here, are historical; the collapse of the shogunal command is a main theme of these chapters.

ch45.anchor: though he had taken three bullets in his body
ch45.note: Hayashi Gonsuke (Yasusada), the old Aizu commissioner of artillery introduced at chapter 43, was mortally wounded directing his guns in the road at Fushimi and died of these wounds during the battle (early February 1868 by the Western calendar). His refusal to be carried to the rear is recorded in Aizu accounts. His son Hayashi Matasaburō, named near the end of this chapter, was killed in the same fighting.

ch45.anchor: the Tōdō clan on the shogunal side
ch45.note: The Tsu domain of the Tōdō house, holding the fortified pass at Yamazaki southwest of Kyoto for the shogunal side, changed sides on the third day and turned its guns on its former allies once the Court had declared Satsuma-Chōshū-Tosa the Imperial army. This defection, opening the shogunal flank, is well attested and was decisive in the rout. There is a bitter irony in the name for readers of this novel: the corpsman Tōdō Heisuke, killed at the Aburanokōji, was of no relation.

ch45.anchor: and this came to the shogunal army swollen in the telling
ch45.note: The nishiki no mihata, the Imperial brocade banner, marked whichever army carried it as the legitimate Imperial force and its enemy as chōteki, rebels against the Throne. Secretly prepared in advance by Ōkubo Toshimichi and Iwakura Tomomi, it was bestowed when Prince Ninnaji-no-miya Yoshiaki was named supreme commander on the fourth day of the First Month (28 January 1868) and raised at the front on the fifth. Its effect was less military than moral: no daimyo wished to be a rebel against the Emperor, and waverers went over or melted away. Shiba makes this — not any defeat in the field — the true breaking of the Tokugawa cause. The banner’s date and effect are well attested; whether its design carried real Imperial sanction from the outset was disputed even at the time.
